claims.text: Nizamabad black pottery is a special kind of clay ware with a dark lustrous body.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad Black pottery is a sp ecial kind of clay ware with a dark lustrous body.

claims.text: The pottery features a shiny black surface with engraved silver patterns.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, line 173
quotes.quote: This particular variety features a shiny black surface with engraved silver patterns.

claims.text: Folkartopedia notes that the black tint comes not from artificial colours or paint but from a number of steps the potter takes.

quotes.quote: Not by artificial colours or paint but this black tint is obtained by a number of steps that the potter takes to finally produce this distinct naturally made black colour.

claims.text: Nizamabad black pottery is a registered geographical indication, which received its GI tag in 2015.

quotes.quote: | Geographical Indications | Nizamabad Black Clay Pottery | | Status | Registered |
it was granted the Geographical Indicator (GI) tag in 2015
FROM APRIL 2015 - MARCH 2016
237 459 Nizamabad Black Pottery Handicrafts Uttar Pradesh

claims.text: Nizamabad, in Azamgarh district of Uttar Pradesh, is renowned for its black pottery.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, line 172
quotes.quote: Nizamabad, in Azamgarh District of Uttar Pradesh, is renowned for its black pottery.
One such different form that combines utility with a unique tradition of decoration is the Black Pottery from Nizamabad, Azamgarh District, Uttar Pradesh.

claims.text: Nizamabad is a small town situated about 100 km (62 miles) north of Varanasi.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad is a small town situated about 100km (62 miles) north of Varanasi

claims.text: Rashmi Pratap describes Nizamabad as a village in Azamgarh, about 80 km from Varanasi.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad, a village in Uttar Pradesh's Azamgarh, about 80 km from Varanasi

claims.text: The 2013 application form says Nizamabad lies on the river Tons, which feeds several lakes on the outskirts of the town.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad is a small town situated about 100km (62 miles) north of Varanasi on the river Tons. which feeds several lakes on the outskirts ofthe town
Dated thls 23d Day of october, 2013

claims.text: The registry gives Uttar Pradesh as the geographical area of the Nizamabad Black Clay Pottery indication.

quotes.quote: | Goods | Handicraft | | Geographical Area | Uttar Pradesh |

claims.text: The GI journal says the Nizamabad black pottery cluster is scattered generally across all parts of Azamgarh district.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad Black pottery cluster is scattered generally a ll parts of Azamgarh district.

claims.text: The October 2013 application form named the whole of Azamgarh and Mau districts as the product's geographical area.

quotes.quote: Whole Azamgarh and Mau districts of Uttar pradesh is the geographical area of this product.
Dated thls 23d Day of october, 2013

claims.text: The GI application states that this kind of pottery originated in the Kutch region of Gujarat.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, line 147
quotes.quote: The art of making this kind of pottery originated in the Kutch region of Gujarat.

claims.text: It is believed that the craft was brought to Nizamabad during the reign of the Mughals.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 147-148
quotes.quote: It is believed to have been brought to Nizamabad during the reign of the Mughals.

claims.text: The GI application says Muslim invaders attacked the town, originally called Hanumantgarh, in the mid-17th century and renamed it Nizamabad.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, lines 176-177
quotes.quote: In the mid-17th century Muslim invaders a ttacked this town, which was originally called Hanumantgarh (Hindu), changing the name to Nizamabad.
The town was called Hanumantgarh that was renamed by the invaders as Nizamabad.

claims.text: The GI application says that early in the 19th century a feudal ruler of the town invited potters from Gujarat to live there in exchange for land.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, lines 177-179
quotes.quote: Early in the 19th century one of its feudal rulers invited potters from Gujarat to come and live here in exchange for land.

claims.text: The GI application says the potters were asked to provide pots for pouring and holding water, and the shapes of the pots gradually became influenced by Muslim forms.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, lines 180-182
quotes.quote: The potters were asked to provide pots for pouring and holding wate r, and gradually the shapes of the pots became influenced by Muslim forms.

claims.text: The GI application says the decorative silver inlay developed through the influence of bidri metalwork brought by Muslims from Hyderabad.

quotes.locator: p. 8, H) Proof of Origin, lines 182-184
quotes.quote: The hi ghly decorative silver inlay incorporated into the pottery here has developed through the influence of bidri metalwork brought in by the Muslims from Hyderabad.

claims.text: Handmade in India, as quoted in Ceramics Technical, says the potters' ancestors came from Gujarat with Abdul Farah Nizamabadi in Emperor Alamgarh's reign, 400 years ago.

quotes.quote: According to historical accounts the art of black pottery came from Gujarat. The ancestors of the potters had accompanied Abdul Farah Nizamabadi to the village during the reign of Emperor Alamgarh, 400 years ago.

claims.text: Sohit Kumar Prajapati said that over 300 years ago, under the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, some clay potters from Kutch migrated and settled at Nizamabad.

quotes.quote: Over 300 years ago during the reign of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, some clay potters from Kutch (Gujarat) had migrated to Azamgarh and settled at Nizamabad to earn living.

claims.text: A Nizamabad potter told Rashmi Pratap that his ancestors came from Gujarat about 500 years ago.

quotes.quote: Surendra's ancestors came from Gujarat, he says, about 500 years back and settled in what is now Uttar Pradesh.

claims.text: Ceramics Technical notes that, as with other crafts, no records are available of the origins of Nizamabad black pottery.

quotes.quote: Like all crafts, there are no available records as to its origins.

claims.text: It is usually said that the craft is more than 500 years old.

quotes.quote: It is usually said that the craft is more than 500 years old.

claims.text: It is believed that a qazi brought the craft of black pottery from Kutch to Nizamabad during the rule of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.

quotes.quote: It is believed that black pottery took root in Nizamabad due to a qazi's efforts during the rule of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. The qazi brought the art and craft of black pottery from Kutch, Gujarat, where it was first developed.

claims.text: A Nizamabad potter recounts the elders' story that a kaji sahib in the Mughal administration, impressed by Prajapati black pottery in Gujarat, brought some artisans to Uttar Pradesh and gave them land.

quotes.quote: We have been hearing from our elders that once a kaji sahib (judge) in the Mughal administration saw black pottery by the Prajapati community in Gujarat. He was so impressed by the work that he brought some artisans to Uttar Pradesh, gave them land for housing and agriculture

claims.text: According to mythological beliefs, feudal rulers influenced by the Persian style called artisans to live in the town and make utensils.

quotes.quote: According to mythological beliefs, the feudal rulers, influenced by the Persian style, had called artisans to live in this city to make utensils, fruits.

claims.text: The Azamgarh district page says that later, talented artisans discovered the technique of adding black colour through ash and smoke.

quotes.quote: Later, talented artisans discovered the technique of adding black color through ash and smoke, which brought fame to this craft.

claims.text: Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati says the British gave a certificate for good work in 1905 to an Azamgarh product made with the naqqashi technique.

quotes.quote: In 1905, there is a certificate for good work given by the British for a product made from Azamgarh using the Naqqashi technique.

claims.text: Traditionally only Prajapatis were potters, and the skill was passed on from one generation to another.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, only Prajapatis were potters and the skill was passed on from one generation to another.

claims.text: Local people say the Prajapati community has been making this pottery since the beginning.

quotes.quote: According to the local people, the Prajapati community has been making this pottery since the beginning.

claims.text: Azamgarh potter Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati received the National Award for Master Craftsman from the Government of India in 2004.

quotes.quote: Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati received the National Award for Master Craftsman from the Government of India in 2004.

The method of making as Ram Jatan rattles off with veritable ease saying, "come to Azamgarh and you can view it first hand." I am not so sure, but try to follow the process. I have seen the pots being made locally by another Azamgarh potter in Delhi.

claims.text: Sohit Kumar Prajapati is a state awardee of the Nizamabad black pottery craft.

quotes.quote: said Sohit Kumar Prajapati, a state awardee of the craft
Present were craftsmen who were awardees Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati, Mrs Pushpa Devi and Sohit Kumar Prajapati.

claims.text: The GI journal's method of production lists the first steps in order: clay procured from local ponds, beaten to a fine powder and wedged, then formed into objects.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 189
quotes.quote: The clay is procured from local ponds.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 190
quotes.quote: The dry lumps of clay are beaten to a fine powder, water is added and the clay is wedged by foot

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 193
quotes.quote: The Objects are then formed.

claims.text: The GI journal's description of the goods lists the later steps in order: baking, a vegetable wash, oil burnishing, twig decoration, smoke firing, oiling and baking again, filling the grooves, then washing and polishing.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 153-155
quotes.quote: After the clay moul d is given a desired shape, the items are baked in fire and then are washed with powered vegetable matter. The surface is then burnished with mustard oil after which a sh arp twig is used fo r decoration.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 156-159
quotes.quote: After following these procedures, the clay wares are then set to smoke firing which gives them the black luster. After creating the objects, the items are rubbed with oil and then baked once again. The grooves of the design are then fill ed in by hand with a fine silvery powder.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 160-161
quotes.quote: When the silvery powder is washed with wa ter and polished, the clay wares exude a silvery hue against the black background of the terracotta.

claims.text: Potters dig clay from ponds in summer, during the dry months of April and May, and store it at home for use through the year.

quotes.quote: In Nizamabad, potters dig out clay from ponds during the dry months of April and May and store it inside their houses for use throughout the year.
The potters procure the clay during the summer months and store it in their homes for use throughout the year.
The mud for the pots is brought from ponds.

claims.text: Dry lumps of clay are beaten to a fine powder, water is added, and the clay is wedged by foot and then by hand to remove stones and coarse material.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, lines 190-191
quotes.quote: The dry lumps of clay are beaten to a fine powder, water is added and the clay is wedged by foot and then by hand whilst re moving any stones and coarse material.

claims.text: In the potters' units the clay is filtered into small pits, mixed with water and left for some days until it thickens, then kneaded lump-free.

quotes.quote: Their units have small pits into which the clay is filtered, mixed with water and left for some days. When it thickens, the clay is kneaded by feet or using machines to make it lump-free.

claims.text: One potter kneads the soaked clay with his feet, then after about 15 minutes kneads it further by hand to improve its elasticity.

quotes.quote: The clay has been soaking in water in the pit for some days and is now thick enough to be kneaded using feet
After about 15 minutes of kneading, a portion of the clay is lifted to a plain surface and further kneaded with hands to improve elasticity.

claims.text: Ceramics Technical describes the mud being soaked, turned fine in a chakki or stone grinder, sieved several times and kneaded with about 40 percent water.

quotes.quote: The mud is soaked in water and in a chakki or a stone grinder turned to make it fine.
The dry mud is powdered. It is sieved several times
The mud is then kneaded with water. Approximately 40 percent of water is added to the mix.

claims.text: The articles are shaped on potter's wheels; most wheels are turned by hand, though electric wheels are also used.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, lines 195-196
quotes.quote: The craftsmen make articles out of clay which has a very fine texture and shapes very well to different forms on potter's wheels.
Most potters work with wheels that turn by the hand. Electric wheels are also used.

claims.text: The shaped object is removed from the wheel with a piece of thread and dried in the sun.

quotes.quote: The object is shaped on the wheel and removed using a piece of thread. It is now dried in the sun.

claims.text: The pottery is partly dried in the sun to keep some moisture, then goes back on the wheel for kharat, peeling off uneven surfaces.

quotes.quote: the handmade pottery is partially dried in the sun to retain some moisture. It goes back on the wheel for 'kharat' or peeling off uneven surfaces.
A second round on the potter's wheel ensures removal, via scraping, of any anomalies in the shape
It is again turned on the wheel, smoothed using a cutter, burnished stone and a few other implements.

claims.text: Handmade in India, as quoted in Ceramics Technical, says thrown pots are dried and smoothed with ghont, a quartz river stone.

quotes.quote: Thrown pots are dried and smoothed with ghont, a quartz river stone.

claims.text: The dried piece is smoothed with a cutter and a burnished stone, then rubbed with an old piece of pure cotton cloth until it feels almost silken.

quotes.quote: It is again turned on the wheel, smoothed using a cutter, burnished stone and a few other implements.
Now an old piece of pure cotton cloth is taken out and the piece is rubbed with it. It now gets a sheen and looks and feels almost silken.

claims.text: After shaping, the items are baked in fire; unfired clay is called kachcha, uncooked, and fired clay becomes pakka, cooked.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, lines 197-199
quotes.quote: After the clay mould is given a desired shape, the items are baked in fire (clay in its unfired state is considered kachcha: uncooked; once fired it becomes pakka: cooked

claims.text: After the first baking, the items are washed with powdered vegetable matter.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 153-154
quotes.quote: After the clay moul d is given a desired shape, the items are baked in fire and then are washed with powered vegetable matter.

claims.text: The washed surface of the pottery is then burnished with mustard oil.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 200
quotes.quote: The surface is then burnished with mustard oil

claims.text: Floral and geometric designs are then incised on the oiled surface with a sharp twig for decoration.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, lines 200-201
quotes.quote: The surface is then burnished with mustard oil after which a sharp twig is used for decoration. Various beautiful floral and geometric designs are then itched to it.
intricate carvings are made through sharpened wooden sticks

claims.text: The intricate geometric and floral patterns are drawn on the pottery with a fine iron needle.

quotes.quote: A fine iron needle is then used to draw intricate geometrical and floral patterns on the pottery.
using a fine needle, carve the patterns on the dried clay

claims.text: The patterns are usually carved by the women of the household, though men are also experts at this work.

quotes.quote: Women usually do this fine work though men also are experts in the art.
Then, the women of the household get together and, using a fine needle, carve the patterns on the dried clay
Engraving is done freehand by the women with a paste of mercury, lead and zinc.

claims.text: To get the glowing black effect, the pottery is dipped into a slip of clay mixed with vegetable matter.

quotes.quote: To get the glowing black glazed effect, the pottery is dipped into a slip made of clay, mixed with vegetable matter.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, lines 202-203
quotes.quote: A pot is dipped in a thin liquid matter of clay mixed with a particular vegetable material.
The sheen is obtained by dipping it into a solution of clay, vegetable matter, dried, then rubbed with a vegetable oil and fired.

claims.text: In one potter's account, kavis, a colour made of clay and water, is applied and the pottery is then left to dry.

quotes.quote: Kavis, a colour made using clay and water, is applied and the pottery is then left to dry.

claims.text: In the account given to Ceramics Technical, the dipping solution is a local yellow mud, peeli mithi, with mango bark, natural leaves and caustic soda.

quotes.quote: The solution is made using a local peeli mithi or yellow mud which is similar to fueller's earth. To the solution apart from the peeli mithi, proportions of mango bark, natural leaves and caustic soda are added.

claims.text: Cow dung fuels the firing, and in one account the oven, or bhatti, is fully covered with cow dung cakes.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 194
quotes.quote: Designs are etched or painted, and the objects fired in ovens fuelled with cow dung.
The pottery then goes inside the bhatti (oven), which is then fully covered with cow dung cakes.

claims.text: The articles are fired with rice husks in an enclosed kiln.

quotes.quote: the articles are fired in enclosed kiln with rice husks

claims.text: Ceramics Technical describes the pieces stacked in an earthen pot packed with wood, cow dung and saw dust, sealed, and lowered into a wood-fired kiln.

quotes.quote: The pieces to be baked are stacked in an earthen pot and filled with wooden pieces, cow dung and saw dust in the empty spaces. The mouth of the pot is then sealed. This is then lowered into the woodfired kiln and allowed to bake.

claims.text: Handmade in India describes firing in an open kiln, with dung cakes placed between the wares and the heap covered with straw and mud.

quotes.quote: Firing is done in an open kiln by placing dung cakes between the wares and covering the heap with straw and mud.

claims.text: Ceramics Technical gives the baking as 750 degrees Celsius for six to eight hours.

quotes.quote: It is baked at 750[degrees]C for six to eight hours time.

claims.text: In one potter's account the oven cools down after 10 to 12 hours, and then the pottery is removed.

quotes.quote: The oven cools down after 10 to 12 hours and then pottery is removed.

claims.text: Outlook Traveller describes a fuel-intensive firing of about 15 days in the kiln, locally called aawan, that produces about 300 pieces.

quotes.quote: A fuel-intensive method, which involves baking the clay pieces for about 15 days in the furnace or kiln or, aawan, as it is locally called, produces about 300 pieces.

claims.text: After the smoke firing, the items are rubbed with oil and baked once again.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 156-158
quotes.quote: After following these procedures, the clay wares are then set to smoke firing which gives them the black luster. After creating the objects, the items are rubbed with oil and then baked once again.

claims.text: The grooves of the design are then filled in by hand with a fine silvery powder.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, line 159
quotes.quote: The grooves of the design are then fill ed in by hand with a fine silvery powder.

claims.text: The filled designs are washed with water and polished so the silvery powder sticks and shows a silvery hue against the black background.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 160-161
quotes.quote: When the silvery powder is washed with wa ter and polished, the clay wares exude a silvery hue against the black background of the terracotta.
Water is then applied, rubbed and applied again to ensure that the silvery powder sticks permanently on the carved design

claims.text: Some vessels are coated with lacquer while still hot from the kiln, which gives them a glossy look and enhances their lustre.

quotes.quote: To lend a glossy look to the products, some vessels are coated with lacquer when still hot.
The lacquer application enhances the black pottery's lustre while it is still hot from the kiln.

claims.text: Dishes and tea sets meant for use as crockery are double fired, in an open kiln and in a closed kiln.

quotes.quote: Double firing in an open kiln and a closed kiln is done for dishes and tea sets used as crockery.

claims.text: Ceramics Technical states that making an object takes three to five days, whatever the number of pieces being made.

quotes.quote: The making of an object takes three to five days, irrespective of the number of pieces to be made.

claims.text: The craftsmen work a clay of very fine texture that shapes very well to different forms.

quotes.locator: p. 8, F) Description of the Goods, lines 150-151
quotes.quote: The craftsmen make articles out of the clay which has a very fine texture and shapes very well to different forms.

claims.text: The clay from the local ponds of Nizamabad is rich in mica.

quotes.quote: The mica-rich clay from the local ponds of Nizamabad is ideal for the pottery practised here
This area's clay has high mica content and has a very fine texture, giving a good finish to the products

claims.text: A 1998 study of Nizamabad clays names Dhuripur, Bhairopur and Nasirpur pond clays among the existing plastic clays used to produce black pottery.

quotes.quote: Prasad, C S and Maiti, Kedar Nath (1998) Physico-chemical characterisation of some common clays of Nizamabad, UP and their utilization in the production of black pottery.
the existing plastic clays like Dhuripur, Bhairopur and Nasirpur pond clays for the production of black pottery

claims.text: The study found that Nasirpur field clay could be used up to 100% as a complete replacement for those pond clays.

quotes.quote: the alternative raw material, namely, Nasirpur field clay could be used even up to 100% in complete replacement of the existing plastic clays

claims.text: The clay is mixed with goat excreta, a widely available local product.

quotes.locator: p. 9, I) Method of Production, line 192

lede.text: Nizamabad black pottery is a clay ware with a dark lustrous body and a shiny black surface engraved with silver patterns, made at Nizamabad in Azamgarh district of Uttar Pradesh.

Folkartopedia notes that its black is not paint, Handmade in India credits a clay slip and reduction firing, and other sources describe smoke trapped during the firing and oxygen kept out of the kiln.
The incised designs are filled with a silvery powder that sources describe as tin, as mercury and tin, as zinc and mercury, as lead, zinc and mercury, or as glass, zinc and mercury.
Traditionally made by Prajapati potters, it is a registered geographical indication that received its GI tag in 2015.

keyFacts.label: Black colour
keyFacts.value: A clay slip and reduction firing in Handmade in India; trapped smoke and an oxygen-free kiln in other accounts

keyFacts.label: Silvery inlay
keyFacts.value: Sources differ: tin; mercury and tin; zinc and mercury; lead, zinc and mercury; or glass, zinc and mercury

keyFacts.label: Firing
keyFacts.value: Six to eight hours at 750 degrees Celsius; the oven cools after 10 to 12 hours; or about 15 days, as sources differ

sentences.text: The GI application states that this kind of pottery originated in the Kutch region of Gujarat, and that early in the 19th century a feudal ruler of the town invited potters from Gujarat in exchange for land.
Other accounts date the potters' arrival differently: Handmade in India to 400 years ago, a state awardee to over 300 years ago under Aurangzeb, and a potter to about 500 years ago.
Ceramics Technical notes that no records are available of the origins of Nizamabad black pottery.
The GI application links the silver inlay to bidri metalwork brought by Muslims from Hyderabad, and says the shapes of the pots gradually became influenced by Muslim forms.
Traditionally only Prajapatis were potters, and the skill was passed on from one generation to another.
Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati received the National Award for Master Craftsman in 2004, and Sohit Kumar Prajapati is a state awardee of the craft.
Ram Jatan says the British gave a certificate for good work in 1905 to an Azamgarh product made with the naqqashi technique.
Nizamabad, in Azamgarh district of Uttar Pradesh, is renowned for its black pottery.
The GI journal places the small town about 100 km north of Varanasi, while another account calls Nizamabad a village about 80 km from Varanasi.
The GI journal says the black pottery cluster is scattered generally across all parts of Azamgarh district.
The registry gives the geographical area as Uttar Pradesh, while the 2013 application form named the whole of Azamgarh and Mau districts.
Potters dig clay from ponds in the dry months of April and May and store it at home for use through the year.
The dry clay is beaten to a fine powder, mixed with water and goat excreta, wedged by foot and by hand, and shaped on potter's wheels.

The GI journal's description of the goods has the shaped items baked, washed with vegetable matter, burnished with mustard oil and decorated with floral and geometric designs before smoke firing, then rubbed with oil and baked again.
The grooves of the design are then filled by hand with a fine silvery powder, washed with water and polished.

Sources differ on this order: the same journal elsewhere, and Kamaladevi Chattopadyay, have the pattern incised after the firing, while other accounts describe the ware dipped in a slip, dried and rubbed with oil before it is fired.
Accounts of the firing differ: an enclosed kiln with rice husks, an open kiln with dung cakes between the wares, or a sealed earthen pot inside a wood-fired kiln.
They also differ on its length, from six to eight hours at 750 degrees Celsius, to the oven cooling after 10 to 12 hours, to about 15 days.
Some vessels are coated with lacquer while still hot from the kiln, which gives them a glossy look.
The clay from the local ponds of Nizamabad is rich in mica and has a very fine texture that shapes very well to different forms.
A 1998 study names Dhuripur, Bhairopur and Nasirpur pond clays among the existing plastic clays and found that Nasirpur field clay could replace them completely.
The slip contains mango bark and bamboo leaves, with aarush or adhatoda leaves by the district's account, or adusath leaves in Handmade in India.
Mustard oil is rubbed on the pottery before firing to make it shinier and smoother.
For the silvery inlay the GI journal names tin, Kamaladevi Chattopadyay mercury and tin, the Times of India zinc and mercury, and other accounts lead, zinc and mercury, or glass, zinc and mercury.
Ceramics Technical reported in 2014 that the availability of good-quality mud was a problem and that it came from villages deeper inside.
Handmade in India attributes the black colour to a clay slip and reduction firing, in which the bark and leaves of the slip carbonise.
The GI journal says the dried pottery, polished with vegetable matter, creates a black oxide when fired, which gives its glowing black surface.
Smoke given off by the fuel and trapped during the firing imparts the black colour.
Potters keep oxygen out of the kiln, because oxygen would turn the pottery red instead of black.

The GI journal lists vases, cups and saucers, dinner sets, water jugs, plates, jars and flower pots among the items made, but Ram Prajapati said potters had stopped making dinner sets and tea sets, so sources differ on whether such tableware is still made.
Potters also make lamps, incense holders and statues of gods and goddesses such as Ganesh, Laxmi, Shiva, Durga and Saraswati.

The GI journal's statement of uniqueness counts surahis among the well admired pots of Nizamabad, but the 2013 application form describes them as glazed pots of Uttar Pradesh with a red-clay base, and Kamaladevi Chattopadyay wrote that the ware cannot hold any liquid.
The designs of flowing lines and floral and geometric patterns are mostly drawn freehand, usually by the women of the household.
This engraving is called naqqashi, and Ceramics Technical counts more than 50 designs, among them jhoomar, bel, paurani, laung and papal.
Parts such as the spout or the handle are cast separately and then attached to the body.
The Yuva Jagriti Pottery Shilp Samiti filed GI application 459 on 31 October 2013, and a state awardee said the potters had the support of NABARD and the Human Welfare Association.
The application was advertised in Geographical Indications Journal 68 on 15 July 2015 and received certificate 237 on 16 November 2015, valid up to 30 October 2033.
The registry's authorised-user list for the indication runs to 53 entries.
In 2014 Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati said around 80 homes made pottery but only three made naqqashi pottery.
Ceramics Technical reported in 2014 that the engraved pottery was made only to order, as the raw materials for the engraving had become prohibitively expensive.
The same report gave para, or mercury, at $200 USD a kilogram and ranga, or zinc, at $100 USD a kilogram.
The pottery is covered by Uttar Pradesh's One District One Product initiative, rolled out in 2018.
